summary:
West Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and those punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. West Sumatra carries no equivalent provincial religious or criminal regime, and its restrictions on LGBT people are written as public-order and administrative measures by cities and regencies.

State and vigilante hostility frame the legal position. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and said the gathering violated no law. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in 2022, was told through his mother in Lima that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists LGBTQ+ people among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled under national defence policy, and reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women.

In West Sumatra, the clearest enacted local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh is Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order. Articles 43-44 prescribe oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. An academic analysis of the regulation in the AHKAM journal reads it as a response to local religious values and Minangkabau customs, examined through Fiqih Siyasah Tanfidziyah.

Enforcement is real but contested. A 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation records supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions judged of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist. A 2025 study records people swept up in LGBT operations or identified through apps rising from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024.

The pattern is spreading to neighbouring regencies. On 13 May 2026 the DPRD of Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) folded into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, carrying administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people, with the drafting body's chair stating the stages had reached finalisation. Customary-law actors are pushing parallel measures, including a boarding-house barcode system and proposed nagari regulations on social deviance.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight Action International's "Creeping Criminalisation" mapping (Katjasungkana and Wieringa) documents discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. West Sumatra is not among them, and the Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping, so the province's newer bylaws sit outside that reference inventory.

The regional bylaw mechanism itself is the relevant structural feature: Indonesian provinces, cities and regencies legislate through Perda and Ranperda on public order, which is how West Sumatra's restrictions reach visitors without any provincial criminal statute on homosexuality.

West Sumatra's instruments differ in kind from Aceh's. Aceh's caning is imposed under provincial religious law and is corporal; Bukittinggi's Perda operates through warnings, administrative fines and rehabilitation, so the immediate exposure for a visitor there is detention, a fine and forced participation in a rehabilitation programme rather than corporal punishment.

The official securitisation of LGBTQ+ people at national level, set out in the October 2025 presidential decree, provides the backdrop against which regency legislatures are finalising draft anti-LGBT regulations and customary institutions are proposing their own measures.
localsOnly:
Satpol PP, the local public order force, carries out supervision, enforcement and guidance under Bukittinggi Perda No. 2 of 2024. A 2026 field study of implementation rates the sanctions as of suboptimal effectiveness and reports that the social rehabilitation component cannot function because the facilities barely exist.

Recorded activity against LGBT people in the province rose sharply: a 2025 study counts individuals swept up in LGBT operations or flagged through app-based findings at 56 in 2023 and 272 in 2024.

Residents face parallel pressure from customary-law bodies. A boarding-house barcode system has been introduced as a screening measure, and nagari (village) authorities have proposed regulations on social deviance that would operate alongside the city and regency bylaws.

The DPRD of Limapuluh Kota regency finalised on 13 May 2026 a Ranperda on public order and tranquility that would impose administrative fines and rehabilitation on LGBT people, with the drafting committee's chair confirming the process had reached finalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bukittinggi Perda No. 2 of 2024 or any other West Sumatra bylaw has been applied to foreign visitors is not sourced in the inventory; the studies cited examine implementation in relation to local populations.

As of the 13 May 2026 report, the Limapuluh Kota instrument is a finalised draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation. Its enactment, commencement date and final penalty schedule remain unresolved in the available sources.

The inventory does not state how the bylaws define the persons they cover, whether the Rp1,000,000 administrative fine in Bukittinggi is the sole monetary penalty, or how many fines, warnings or rehabilitation orders have actually been imposed. No prosecution or penalty data for West Sumatra is available here.

No independent province-wide inventory of West Sumatra regional regulations exists in this material: the OutRight Action International mapping predates the Bukittinggi regulation and does not cover the province, so other cities or regencies with comparable bylaws would not appear in it.
